<reason>Side B won the decisive exchanges. B's trajectory argument (secular sexed codes like heels-and-makeup mandates being dismantled) forced A to explicitly abandon the parity analogy that anchored A's opening ("never claiming parity" [A4.3]), and B correctly identified and weaponized that retreat. B also captured A's "the volunteer unit is the family" framing [A4.1] as a concession that the person bearing the code never consented — the exact argument from B1.4 — and carried it cleanly through the closing ("who volunteers for the burden?"). A mounted real defenses: the structure/content distinction, the "parental proxy choice proves too much" response, and the charge that B's bright line is an extreme categorical ban A identified early and B never fully defended for adult employees. But A dropped the administrability clash after Rebuttal 1, the sex-differentiated-curricula comparison arrived only in closing, and the badge-equivalency exchange ended roughly even after B's "the burden tracks sex, not enrollment" counter. B asked the two sharpest pressure questions, answered A's pressure directly with the A1/A2 format, and made the debate easier to decide; the clipped ending of B4 is a minor execution cost. Clear but competitive win for CON.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.1/B4.4: B quoted A's own words — "the volunteer unit is the family" — to show A conceded that the code-wearer never consented, then showed A's Rebuttal 2 abandoned the parity argument A's opening was built on, converting A's strategic retreat into proof that the resolution seeks an exemption from the scrutiny now catching secular sexed codes.</best_rebuttal>
